title: Walls Against Death: A Close Reading of Poe's Red Death
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: The Masque of the Red Death
source.venue: Graham's Magazine (first published as "The Mask of the Red Death")

intro.summary: Poe's short story asks whether wealth, walls and pleasure can shut out death. A prince seals himself and a thousand courtiers inside an abbey while a plague kills his people outside. At a masked ball, a guest dressed as the plague walks through seven coloured rooms, the prince dies chasing him, and the costume turns out to be empty. The story's answer is that nothing walls out death. Its main limit as 'evidence' is that it is fiction. Readings of the rooms and the clock as symbols of a human life are interpretations that Poe never states outright.
background: Edgar Allan Poe (1809–1849) was an American writer known for short, dark Gothic tales built around a single strong effect.
A 'masque' is a masked ball or courtly entertainment, where guests hide their faces behind costumes.
The 'Red Death' is an invented disease. Poe gives it vivid symptoms, but it matches no real illness.
Readers often treat the story as an allegory, a tale whose objects and places stand for bigger ideas like time, life and death.
intro.aha: The welded gates never kept the plague out: the 'guest' everyone took for a man in costume was empty inside, so death had walked in unseen, and the seal meant to protect the revellers only locked them in with it.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: A terrible plague, the Red Death, is sweeping the land. It kills within half an hour and leaves blood on the victim's face. The story asks a question as old as plagues: can the rich and powerful escape death by locking themselves away?
primer.quote: No pestilence had ever been so fatal, or so hideous.

primer.heading: What Poe did
primer.body: Poe sets up a sealed experiment. Prince Prospero takes a thousand healthy friends into a walled abbey and has the iron gates welded shut. He fills it with food, wine and entertainers. Months later he throws a masked ball across seven rooms, each lit in a single colour. The last room is black, with blood-red windows and a huge ebony clock whose hourly chime makes everyone freeze.
primer.quote: With such precautions the courtiers might bid defiance to contagion. The external world could take care of itself.

primer.heading: What happens
primer.body: At midnight the guests notice a tall figure dressed as a plague victim, with its mask and robes spattered with blood. The furious prince chases it from the blue room through every room to the black one. He falls dead there. When the guests seize the figure, they find nothing inside the costume. Then they all die.
primer.quote: gasped in unutterable horror at finding the grave cerements and corpse-like mask, which they handled with so violent a rudeness, untenanted by any tangible form.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: The story turns a wall into a trap. The seal meant to keep death out ends up keeping the revellers in with it. Its images still shape how people talk about wealth and isolation during epidemics. But it is a work of imagination, not a report. When we read the seven rooms as stages of life or the clock as mortality, that is a well-supported interpretation, not something the text declares.

concepts.title: Within and without: the sealed abbey
concepts.idea: Prospero tries to buy safety by welding himself and his friends inside a wall, splitting the world into a protected 'within' and an abandoned 'without'.

terms.means: A deadly disease that spreads through a whole population; a plague
A building that was once a religious house, fortified with walls like a castle

concepts.recap: Prospero welds a wall between a pleasure-filled 'within' and a plague-ridden 'without', and decides the outside is no longer his concern.

understand.explanation: The story opens by drawing a hard line: outside is a pestilence that kills in half an hour and cuts its victims off from all sympathy. Inside a castellated abbey, behind a wall with welded iron gates, are a thousand healthy friends, food and every kind of pleasure. Prospero builds this line on purpose: he leaves his half-emptied lands to fend for themselves, and his court treats grief and thought as foolish. Everything that follows in the tale happens on the 'within' side of this wall, so keep the split in mind. This is a short story, not a study, so what the wall means is a matter of reading the text. Still, the text itself states the division in plain words.
understand.quote: The prince had provided all the appliances of pleasure. There were buffoons, there were improvisatori, there were ballet-dancers, there were musicians, there was Beauty, there was wine. All these and security were within. Without was the “Red Death”.

activities.prompt: Follow how the story builds its wall, one step at a time.

stages.label: 1. The plague outside
stages.text: A pestilence (a deadly disease sweeping the whole country) called the 'Red Death' is killing people. Victims feel sharp pains, then dizziness, then bleed from their pores, and they die within half an hour. The scarlet stains on a victim's face shut them out 'from the aid and from the sympathy of his fellow-men.' So even before any wall goes up, the sick are already cast out.

stages.label: 2. The retreat
stages.text: When his lands are 'half depopulated', Prince Prospero does not stay with his people. He picks 'a thousand hale and light-hearted friends' from his court, healthy and cheerful ones. He leads them into a castellated abbey: a former religious house with castle-like walls, built to his own strange taste.

stages.label: 3. The welding
stages.text: The abbey has a 'strong and lofty wall' with iron gates. Once inside, the courtiers bring furnaces and heavy hammers and weld the bolts shut. Now nobody can come in, and nobody can rush out on a sudden impulse of despair. The abbey is fully stocked with food.

stages.label: 4. The split
stages.text: Inside are jesters, dancers, musicians, wine and 'security'. Outside is the Red Death. The narrator sums up the court's mood: 'The external world could take care of itself.' Grieving and even thinking are dismissed as folly.

activities.takeaway: Step by step, the prince turns one plague-struck country into two worlds: a sealed 'within' he protects and a 'without' he abandons.

activities.title: Which side of the wall?
activities.prompt: Place each detail from the story on the side of the wall where the story puts it.

cards.text: Buffoons, ballet-dancers and musicians
cards.feedback: Within. These are among the 'appliances of pleasure' the prince provided inside the abbey.

cards.text: Wine
cards.feedback: Within. The story lists 'there was wine' among the pleasures behind the wall.

cards.text: A thousand hale and light-hearted friends
cards.feedback: Within. Prospero chose these healthy, cheerful courtiers to join him. 'Hale' means they were picked from among the well.

cards.text: Security
cards.feedback: Within. The text says 'All these and security were within.' Safety is presented as one more thing the prince keeps inside.

cards.text: The 'Red Death'
cards.feedback: Without. The text says it plainly: 'Without was the “Red Death”.' The whole design of the abbey assumes the plague stays on that side.

cards.text: The prince's subjects in his half-depopulated lands
cards.feedback: Without. Prospero leaves when his dominions are half emptied, and his people stay behind: 'The external world could take care of itself.'

cards.text: Victims shut out from the sympathy of their fellow-men
cards.feedback: Without. The plague already isolates the sick. The wall repeats that exclusion on a larger scale, because nobody inside will help them.

cards.text: Ample provisions of food
cards.feedback: Within. 'The abbey was amply provisioned', so the revellers can stay sealed in for months without needing the outside world.

activities.takeaway: Pleasure, health, food and safety are gathered inside. Disease, the common people and their suffering are left outside. The wall sorts the world just as you did.

activities.question: Which passage best shows the court's attitude toward the people left outside the wall?

options.quote: The external world could take care of itself. In the meantime it was folly to grieve, or to think.
options.feedback: Yes. This states the attitude outright. The outside world is not their responsibility, and even grieving over it or thinking about it is dismissed as foolish.

options.quote: The abbey was amply provisioned. With such precautions the courtiers might bid defiance to contagion.
options.feedback: This shows the courtiers' confidence that supplies and walls keep the disease out. It is about their own safety, not about how they regard the people outside.

options.quote: This was an extensive and magnificent structure, the creation of the prince’s own eccentric yet august taste.
options.feedback: This describes the building and the prince's taste. It says nothing about his attitude toward his abandoned subjects.

options.quote: They resolved to leave means neither of ingress nor egress to the sudden impulses of despair or of frenzy from within.
options.feedback: Close, because it describes the sealing. But it is about blocking any way in or out, including panicked attempts to leave from inside. It shows how sealed the wall is, not what the court thinks of the people outside.

hints: Look for a line about the world beyond the wall, not about the building or its supplies.
Which passage mentions 'the external world'?

concepts.title: Seven rooms from east to west
concepts.idea: The seven rooms run in a fixed colour order from a blue eastern room to a black western room with blood-red windows, so the building itself lays out a path that ends in death.

terms.means: Treating a concrete detail in a story, such as a room's colour, as standing for a larger idea, such as a stage of life
A story whose places, objects or characters can be read as a sustained picture of something beyond the literal events

concepts.recap: Inside the sealed abbey, the prince's seven rooms form a one-way colour path from a bright blue east to a black west lit through blood-red glass, so the house itself points toward death.

understand.explanation: Inside the sealed abbey, the masked ball takes place in seven rooms, and Poe describes them in a strict order from east to west: blue, purple, green, orange, white, violet, and finally black. The rooms have no lamps inside. Fires burn in corridors behind stained-glass windows, and in six rooms the glass matches that room's colour. The seventh, black room breaks the pattern: its windows are scarlet, "a deep blood colour", and few guests dare to enter it. A symbolic reading treats this layout as more than decoration. Read that way, the suite becomes an allegory: a fixed path that runs like the sun from east to west, or like a life from youth to death, and it ends in the colours of the plague. Poe never states what the rooms mean, so these are readings that critics and readers bring to the text, not facts the story declares.
understand.quote: That at the eastern extremity was hung, for example in blue—and vividly blue were its windows. The second chamber was purple in its ornaments and tapestries, and here the panes were purple. The third was green throughout, and so were the casements. The fourth was furnished and lighted with orange—the fifth with white—the sixth with violet.
understand.quote_where: Description of the imperial suite, middle of the story

activities.prompt: Put the seven rooms in order as Poe lays them out, starting at the eastern end and finishing at the western end.
items: Blue room, with vividly blue windows
Black velvet room, with scarlet windows
activities.explanation: Poe names the blue room as the one 'at the eastern extremity' and then counts onward: purple second, green third, orange fourth, white fifth, violet sixth. The seventh, black room is 'the western or black chamber'. It is also where the ebony clock stands. The order is fixed, so moving through the suite always means moving toward the black room.
hints: The story starts its count at the eastern end, and that room is the colour of a clear morning sky.
After blue and purple comes a colour of growing things. Then come three lighter or warmer colours.
The last room is the only one whose windows do not match its walls.

activities.question: Poe never explains the colour sequence. Which reading of the seven rooms do you find most persuasive? Each option's feedback shows what supports it and where it runs out.

options.text: Sunrise to sunset: the rooms follow the sun's path from east to west, from bright morning to the darkness of night.
options.feedback: Supported: Poe takes care to call the blue room 'eastern' and the black room 'western', and the sun rises in the east and sets in the west. Later he notes that 'the night is waning away' as fewer guests visit the black room. Limit: the middle colours, such as green and white, do not match sky colours very well, so this reading explains the two ends better than the middle.

options.text: Birth to death: the rooms are the stages of a human life, ending in the black room where death waits.
options.feedback: Supported: the path is one-way and ends in black and blood red, the colours of death and of the Red Death. The clock that marks passing time stands in that same room, and the guests avoid it, as people avoid thinking about their own end. Limit: the text never names any stages of life. Any exact mapping, such as 'green is youth' or 'white is old age', is a reader's guess and not something Poe says.

options.text: No hidden meaning: the colours are just the prince's strange taste in decoration.
options.feedback: Supported: Poe does say the layout came from 'the duke's love of the bizarre' and that he 'had a fine eye for colours and effects'. Limit: the details pile up in one direction. The black room has blood-coloured glass and holds the clock, guests fear it, and the story's climax happens there. That makes 'mere decoration' hard to sustain, even though the literal explanation is true inside the story.

options.text: The rooms get steadily darker, one shade at a time, from blue to black.
options.feedback: This one rests on a misreading of the text. The fifth room is white, the lightest colour of all, so the suite does not darken step by step. Whatever the sequence means, it is not a smooth fade. The real break comes at the very end, when the black room's scarlet windows depart from the matching rule.

activities.question: Which passage marks the black room as different from the other six?

options.quote: But in this chamber only, the colour of the windows failed to correspond with the decorations. The panes here were scarlet—a deep blood colour.
options.feedback: Yes. Every other room has windows that match its walls, but the black room alone breaks that rule, and it breaks it with the colour of blood. That links the end of the path to the 'redness and the horror of blood' of the plague.

options.quote: These windows were of stained glass whose colour varied in accordance with the prevailing hue of the decorations of the chamber into which it opened.
options.feedback: This passage states the general rule that window colour matches room colour. It sets up the contrast, but it does not single out the black room. The passage that does is the one saying the black room breaks this rule.

options.quote: The third was green throughout, and so were the casements.
options.feedback: This describes an ordinary room where walls and windows match. It shows the pattern the black room will break, but it says nothing about what makes the black room different.

options.quote: There was a sharp turn at every twenty or thirty yards, and at each turn a novel effect.
options.feedback: This applies to the whole suite. Every turn gives a new effect, so the line explains why guests see only one room at a time. It does not set the black room apart.

hints: Look for a passage about one room only, not about the whole suite.
The difference concerns the windows and whether they match the walls.

concepts.title: The clock that stops the dance
concepts.idea: Each hourly chime forces the revel to freeze and remember time, and each time the guests laugh it off and vow not to be shaken again, a repeating cycle of denial.

terms.means: An object or image that reminds people they will die (Latin: 'remember that you must die')

concepts.recap: Every hour the clock makes the revellers remember time, and every hour they laugh and promise to forget. The promise never holds.

understand.explanation: In the black western room, the room at the end of the path, stands a gigantic ebony clock. Every hour its chime is so strange that the orchestra stops, the waltzers freeze, the giddiest guests grow pale and the older, steadier ones pass their hands over their brows as if lost in thought. When the echoes fade, everyone laughs at their own nervousness, and the musicians whisper vows that the next chime will not move them. Sixty minutes later the same thing happens again, in the same way, so the vow never holds. Readers often call an object like this a memento mori, a reminder that you will die. Poe never uses that phrase, so treat it as one reading; what the text itself shows is a loop of reminder, fear and forced forgetting, with the hour spelled out as 3,600 seconds 'of the Time that flies' inside the sealed walls.
understand.quote: But when the echoes had fully ceased, a light laughter at once pervaded the assembly; the musicians looked at each other and smiled as if at their own nervousness and folly, and made whispering vows, each to the other, that the next chiming of the clock should produce in them no similar emotion
understand.quote_where: Paragraph describing the ebony clock in the black chamber

activities.prompt: Put one turn of the clock's cycle in the order Poe describes it.
items: The ebony clock begins to strike the hour
The musicians pause and the waltzers stop dancing
The giddiest grow pale; the older guests pass their hands over their brows
The echoes die away and light laughter spreads through the crowd
The musicians whisper vows that the next chime will not affect them
Sixty minutes later the clock strikes again and the same unease returns
activities.explanation: The order matters. The fear comes while the chimes are still ringing ('while the chimes of the clock yet rang'). The laughter comes only once the echoes have 'fully ceased', so the guests relax because the sound has stopped, not because anything has changed. The vow comes last, and the next chime cancels it. The final step leads straight back to the first, which is what makes this a cycle and not a single event.
hints: Start with the sound itself, then ask what the sound does to the music.
The laughter cannot start until the echoes have ended.
The vow looks forward to the next chime, so it must come just before the next chime arrives.

activities.question: Which passage shows that the musicians' vow fails?

options.quote: and then, after the lapse of sixty minutes, (which embrace three thousand and six hundred seconds of the Time that flies,) there came yet another chiming of the clock, and then were the same disconcert and tremulousness and meditation as before.
options.feedback: Yes. The vow was that the next chime would produce 'no similar emotion'. Here the next chime produces 'the same disconcert and tremulousness and meditation as before', so the promise breaks at the first test. Poe also counts out the seconds, so time is felt passing even inside the sealed abbey.

options.quote: But the echoes of the chime die away—they have endured but an instant—and a light, half-subdued laughter floats after them as they depart.
options.feedback: This is the laughter step of the cycle, the moment of relief. It shows the guests shaking off the chime, not the vow failing. The failure comes when the next chime brings the same fear back. Notice too that the laughter is 'half-subdued', so even the relief is uneasy.

options.quote: But, in spite of these things, it was a gay and magnificent revel.
options.feedback: This line says the party went on despite the chimes. It is close to the guests' own view of things, but it does not show a vow, or a vow breaking.

options.quote: Its pendulum swung to and fro with a dull, heavy, monotonous clang
options.feedback: This describes the clock's steady ticking between the hours. It sets up the clock, but it says nothing about the guests' promise or what happens to it.

hints: First recall what the vow promised: that the next chime would cause 'no similar emotion'.
Look for the passage where the next chime actually arrives and you can see how the guests react.

activities.question: At midnight the clock strikes again, but this time the cycle does not end in laughter. According to the text, what is different about this chime?

options.text: It has twelve strokes, so the pause lasts longer, more thought creeps in, and guests have time to notice something they had missed.
options.feedback: Right. Poe writes that 'there were twelve strokes to be sounded' and that 'more of thought crept, with more of time' into the guests' minds. The longer reminder gives them time to notice a masked figure no one had noticed before. Each hourly chime was too short to break the denial. This one is long enough.

options.text: The guests finally keep their vow and stay calm through the chime.
options.feedback: No. Poe says there was 'an uneasy cessation of all things as before'. The same freeze happens, and the vow fails once more. What changes is how long the freeze lasts.

options.text: The clock stops working, so the music never pauses.
options.feedback: No. The text says 'the music ceased, as I have told'. The clock stops only at the very end of the story, 'with that of the last of the gay'.

options.text: The prince orders the musicians to keep playing over the chime.
options.feedback: The text says nothing like this. The prince does hush the music later with a wave of his hand, but that comes after the midnight chime, when he is angry, and it is not a response to the clock.

hints: Count the strokes of an ordinary hour against the strokes at midnight.
Poe links the number of strokes to how much thought 'crept' into the guests' minds.

concepts.title: The one costume nobody could bear
concepts.idea: At a ball where almost any grotesque costume is allowed, the one disguise the guests cannot tolerate is the plague itself, because it names exactly what the party exists to forget.

terms.means: The freedom the masked ball gives guests to dress and act however they like
A masked or costumed performer; Poe's word for the stranger

concepts.recap: Grotesque, wanton and even corpse-like costumes were tolerated, but dressing as the Red Death itself was not, because it named the one thing the revel existed to forget.

understand.explanation: Prospero's ball is built to be wild. His own taste fills the rooms with costumes that are grotesque, wanton, bizarre and even disgusting, so the night's masquerade licence, its permission to dress as anything, is almost unlimited. The story even says a tall figure in grave clothes with a corpse-like mask 'might have been endured'. What crosses the line is that this mummer, a masked stranger, has dressed as the Red Death itself, with a blood-dabbled robe and a face spattered with scarlet. The guests move from surprise to terror and disgust, and a natural reading is that this costume points straight at the plague the sealed abbey and the revel exist to shut out. That reading is an interpretation: Poe never says it outright, and his narrator says only that some matters are beyond any jest.
understand.quote: In truth the masquerade licence of the night was nearly unlimited; but the figure in question had out-Heroded Herod, and gone beyond the bounds of even the prince’s indefinite decorum.
understand.quote_where: The masked figure appears at midnight (paragraph after the twelve strokes of the clock)

activities.prompt: Set what the ball allows beside what the stranger wears. Look for the one detail that tips the guests from tolerance into horror.

cases.label: What the ball allows
cases.text: The prince's own taste shaped the costumes. There were 'arabesque figures with unsuited limbs', 'delirious fancies such as the madman fashions', 'much of the bizarre, something of the terrible, and not a little of that which might have excited disgust.' The guests are called 'a multitude of dreams.'

cases.label: The stranger, part one
cases.text: Tall and gaunt, 'shrouded from head to foot in the habiliments of the grave', with a mask so like 'a stiffened corpse' that close study could hardly detect the cheat. The narrator says: 'all this might have been endured, if not approved.'

cases.label: The stranger, part two
cases.text: 'But the mummer had gone so far as to assume the type of the Red Death.' His robe is 'dabbled in blood' and his face 'besprinkled with the scarlet horror', the same scarlet stains the story's opening describes on plague victims.

activities.takeaway: Death as a theme is tolerated. The specific marks of the Red Death are not. The line falls between death in general and the plague raging outside the walls.

activities.title: Endured or beyond the bounds?
activities.prompt: Sort each costume detail by how the story says the revellers treat it.

cards.text: Arabesque figures with mismatched limbs
cards.feedback: Endured. These are among the prince's own grotesque designs for the night.

cards.text: Costumes that might have excited disgust
cards.feedback: Endured. The story lists 'not a little of that which might have excited disgust' among the ordinary maskers, so disgust alone is not what crosses the line.

cards.text: Something of the terrible
cards.feedback: Endured. Terror in costume was part of the revel's palette.

cards.text: Grave clothes from head to foot
cards.feedback: Endured, which surprises many people. The narrator says 'all this might have been endured, if not approved.' Death imagery on its own was not the problem.

cards.text: A mask like a stiffened corpse
cards.feedback: Endured, by the same sentence. A corpse mask is grim, but it still falls inside the night's licence.

cards.text: A robe dabbled in blood
cards.feedback: Beyond the bounds. Blood is the Red Death's 'Avatar and its seal'. This is the moment the mummer 'assume[s] the type of the Red Death.'

cards.text: A face spattered with scarlet
cards.feedback: Beyond the bounds. The opening calls scarlet stains on the face 'the pest ban' that marks a victim. The costume copies the plague's own signature.

activities.takeaway: Everything up to a corpse in grave clothes stays inside the licence. Only the plague's specific signs, blood and scarlet stains, push the costume past what anyone will bear.

activities.question: Based on the story, why is this costume the one the guests cannot bear?

options.text: It is the most disgusting costume at the ball.
options.feedback: Not supported. Costumes 'which might have excited disgust' were already present and tolerated. Disgust alone does not explain the line.
Not supported. The narrator says the grave clothes and corpse mask 'might have been endured.' Death in general was allowed.

options.text: It copies the Red Death, the very plague the revellers sealed themselves away to escape and forget.
options.feedback: Supported. The line is crossed only when the mummer 'assume[s] the type of the Red Death', with the blood and scarlet stains the story's opening gives the disease. The prince calls it 'blasphemous mockery'.

options.text: It clashed with the prince's colour scheme.
options.feedback: Not supported. The text gives no hint that the reaction is about style. The prince's rage is aimed at the insult of mocking the plague.

hints: Look again at which details the narrator says 'might have been endured'.
What do the blood and the scarlet stains copy from the story's first paragraph?

activities.question: The narrator says that even for 'the utterly lost, to whom life and death are equally jests, there are matters of which no jest can be made.' What does the guests' horror suggest about them?

options.text: Their carefree mood was always partly a cover. Like the pauses at each chime, the costume shows the fear they had been laughing off.
options.feedback: Well supported. It links to the clock: each chime made 'the giddiest' grow pale before they laughed it away. The costume is a chime that cannot be laughed off. Still, the text describes their feelings only from outside.

options.text: They are offended on moral grounds. Mocking a plague that is killing people outside is simply in bad taste.
options.feedback: Partly supported. The company feels the costume has 'neither wit nor propriety', and the prince calls it 'blasphemous mockery'. This reading fits less well with the guests' terror, which goes beyond offence.

options.text: They are reacting only to surprise at an uninvited guest.
options.feedback: Weakly supported. Surprise is the first note ('disapprobation and surprise'), but the reaction escalates to 'terror, of horror, and of disgust', which surprise alone does not explain.

concepts.title: The empty mask: death was already inside
concepts.idea: The stranger walks the full path of rooms to the black chamber, the prince dies there, and the costume proves empty: the plague itself had come in, so the seal only trapped the revellers with it.

terms.means: An old word for a masked actor or costumed performer; the story uses it for the stranger in the Red Death disguise
Here, an outcome that is the opposite of what someone planned: the thing built to save you is what dooms you

concepts.recap: The welded gates never kept the plague out: the 'guest' was empty inside, so the seal meant to protect the revellers only locked them in with death.

understand.explanation: The prince orders the stranger seized, but no one dares, so the figure walks the whole chain of rooms from the blue room to the black one. Prospero chases it with a dagger, and he drops dead the moment it turns to face him. When the guests finally grab the mummer, they find only the shroud and the mask, with no body inside. The figure was never a man in costume: it was the Red Death itself, already within the walls. That is the story's irony. The welded gates, meant to keep contagion out, now leave no way out for anyone, and every reveller dies inside. Poe never explains how the plague got in. 'Like a thief in the night' is his phrase, and reading the walls as a trap is an interpretation of the story's logic, not a fact the text states.
understand.quote: And now was acknowledged the presence of the Red Death. He had come like a thief in the night. And one by one dropped the revellers in the blood-bedewed halls of their revel, and died each in the despairing posture of his fall.

activities.prompt: Follow the last minutes of the masquerade, one moment at a time.

stages.label: 1. The order nobody obeys
stages.text: In the blue eastern room, Prospero shouts: "Seize him and unmask him!" His courtiers start forward, then stop. A nameless awe holds them back. The stranger, a mummer dressed as the Red Death, passes within a yard of the prince, and the crowd shrinks back to the walls.

stages.label: 2. The walk along the path
stages.text: With slow, measured steps, the figure goes from blue to purple, to green, to orange, to white, to violet. This is the fixed east-to-west route the building lays out, and it ends in the black room with blood-red windows.

stages.label: 3. The chase into the black room
stages.text: Ashamed of his own fear, Prospero rushes through the six rooms with a drawn dagger. No one follows him. At the far end of the black velvet room, the figure turns to face him. There is a sharp cry, the dagger falls, and the prince drops dead on the black carpet.

stages.label: 4. The unmasking
stages.text: Desperate, a crowd of revellers throws itself into the black room and seizes the figure standing by the ebony clock. They tear at the grave clothes and the corpse-like mask, and they find nothing inside. No body, no man. The costume was empty.

stages.label: 5. The last chime
stages.text: Now everyone understands what came in. The revellers fall one by one in the halls of their party. The ebony clock stops with the last of them, and the fires in the tripods go out.

stages.label: 6. What the walls really did
stages.text: Go back to the welded iron gates. They were meant to keep the plague out. They never did. The 'guest' everyone took for a man in costume was empty inside, so death had walked in unseen. And since the bolts left no way in or out, the seal meant to protect the revellers only locked them in with it.

activities.takeaway: The abbey's protection turned around completely: once death was inside, the wall that shut out the world also shut in everyone with the plague.

activities.question: Which passage shows that the stranger was not a man in a costume but the plague itself?

options.quote: gasped in unutterable horror at finding the grave cerements and corpse-like mask, which they handled with so violent a rudeness, untenanted by any tangible form.
options.feedback: Yes. 'Untenanted by any tangible form' means no one was inside the costume. The figure was not a reveller in disguise, so the disguise was the Red Death itself.

options.quote: With such precautions the courtiers might bid defiance to contagion.
options.feedback: This is the courtiers' hope at the start, from before the ball. It tells us what they believed the walls would do, not what came in. The ending proves that belief wrong.

options.quote: there were many individuals in the crowd who had found leisure to become aware of the presence of a masked figure which had arrested the attention of no single individual before.
options.feedback: This shows the figure arrived without anyone noticing, which is a strong clue. But at this point everyone still assumes a person is under the mask. Only the unmasking shows the costume is empty.

options.quote: The external world could take care of itself.
options.feedback: This describes the courtiers' attitude toward the people left outside. It says nothing about the stranger. Its irony only becomes clear once death turns out to be inside, not outside.

hints: Look for the moment the revellers actually touch the figure.
Which line says what was, or wasn't, under the mask?

activities.title: Shelter or trap?
activities.prompt: Sort each of Prospero's arrangements by what it did in the end.

cards.text: Welding the bolts of the iron gates shut
cards.feedback: The courtiers left 'means neither of ingress nor egress.' That was meant to stop despair from breaking out. Once death was inside, it meant no one could escape.

cards.text: Stocking the abbey with ample provisions
cards.feedback: The supplies let the court live in seclusion for five or six months. They bought time, but food could not keep out what finally came.

cards.text: Holding a masked ball where almost any costume was allowed
cards.feedback: The 'nearly unlimited' licence of the masquerade let the plague walk among the guests looking like one more costume. Nobody noticed it until midnight.

cards.text: Musicians, dancers, buffoons and wine
cards.feedback: These made the months inside pleasant and kept grief away. They comforted people but offered no protection. The music simply stopped when the clock struck.

cards.text: Packing a thousand friends together in the crowded rooms
cards.feedback: The rooms were 'densely crowded' with the whole court. When the Red Death showed itself, there was no one beyond its reach. The revellers fell 'one by one' in their own halls.

activities.takeaway: Even the comforts that helped only delayed the end. The very features of the shelter (sealed gates, licence to disguise, a crowd shut in together) are what let death in unnoticed and kept everyone with it.
hints: Ask of each one: did it matter once the plague was inside?
The gates, the costumes and the crowd all mattered at midnight. Food and music did not.

activities.question: By the end of the story, what had the welded gates actually done?

options.text: Kept the plague out. The prince died of shock, and the others of fear.
options.feedback: The text rules this out. The empty costume and the line 'now was acknowledged the presence of the Red Death' show the plague itself was inside, not just fear of it.

options.text: Failed to keep the plague out, and then left the revellers no way to escape it.
options.feedback: Supported. Death came in 'like a thief in the night' as a figure everyone took for a guest. With the bolts welded and no means of egress, all the revellers died inside the walls.

options.text: Protected everyone except Prospero, who was killed for chasing the figure.
options.feedback: Not supported. The prince dies first, but then 'one by one dropped the revellers.' The story ends with the last of them dead and the clock stopped.

options.text: Showed that the plague had been hiding inside the abbey from the very start.
options.feedback: The text never says when or how the Red Death got in, only that it 'had come like a thief in the night.' The story's point is that walls could not stop it, not a precise timeline of its entry.

hints: Remember who dies at the end: just the prince, or everyone?
Think about what 'neither ingress nor egress' means once the danger is already inside.
